title: improved costs and outcomes with conscious sedation vs general anesthesia in tavr patients: time to wake up?
display_name: Improved costs and outcomes with conscious sedation vs general anesthesia in TAVR patients: Time to wake up?
abstract: conscious sedation is emerging as a safe and viable option for anesthesia in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement. the use of conscious sedation was not only associated with similar rates of adverse events, but also shortened icu and overall hospital stays. finally, there were significant decreases in all cost categories when compared to a propensity matched cohort receiving general anesthesia.

title: association between surgical indications, operative risk, and clinical outcome in infective endocarditis
display_name: Association Between Surgical Indications, Operative Risk, and Clinical Outcome in Infective Endocarditis
abstract: background use of surgery for the treatment of infective endocarditis (ie) as related to surgical indications and operative risk for mortality has not been well defined. methods and results the international collaboration on endocarditis plus (ice-plus) is a prospective cohort of consecutively enrolled patients with definite ie from 29 centers in 16 countries. we included patients from ice-plus with definite left-sided, non cardiac device related ie who were enrolled between september 1, 2008, and december 31, 2012. a total of 1296 patients with left-sided ie were included. surgical treatment was performed in 57% of the overall cohort and in 76% of patients with a surgical indication. reasons for nonsurgical treatment included poor prognosis (33.7%), hemodynamic instability (19.8%), death before surgery (23.3%), stroke (22.7%), and sepsis (21%). among patients with a surgical indication, surgical treatment was independently associated with the presence of severe aortic regurgitation, abscess, embolization before surgical treatment, and transfer from an outside hospital. variables associated with nonsurgical treatment were a history of moderate/severe liver disease, stroke before surgical decision, and staphyloccus aureus etiology. the integration of surgical indication, society of thoracic surgeons ie score, and use of surgery was associated with 6-month survival in ie. conclusions surgical decision making in ie is largely consistent with established guidelines, although nearly one quarter of patients with surgical indications do not undergo surgery. operative risk assessment by society of thoracic surgeons ie score provides prognostic information for survival beyond the operative period. s aureus ie was significantly associated with nonsurgical management.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Clinical Medicine > Surgery > Cardiovascular Surgery

title: use of preoperative gabapentin significantly reduces postoperative opioid consumption: a meta-analysis
display_name: Use of preoperative gabapentin significantly reduces postoperative opioid consumption: a meta-analysis
abstract: the administration of preoperative gabapentin reduced the consumption of opioids during the initial 24 hours following surgery. the reduction in postoperative opioids with preoperative gabapentin increased postoperative somnolence, but no significant differences were observed in nausea and vomiting incidences. the results from this study demonstrate that gabapentin is more beneficial in mastectomy and spinal, abdominal, and thyroid surgeries. gabapentin is an effective analgesic adjunct, and clinicians should consider its use in multimodal treatment plans among patients undergoing elective surgery.

title: creation of an atrial septal defect in utero for fetuses with hypoplastic left heart syndrome and intact or highly restrictive atrial septum
display_name: Creation of an Atrial Septal Defect In Utero for Fetuses With Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome and Intact or Highly Restrictive Atrial Septum
abstract: background infants born with hypoplastic left heart syndrome and an intact or highly restrictive atrial septum face a neonatal mortality of at least 48% despite early postnatal left atrial decompression and palliative surgery. prenatal left atrial decompression has been suggested as a means of improving these outcomes. this study reports the feasibility of fetal catheterization to create an interatrial communication and describes technical considerations. methods and results seven fetuses at 26 to 34 weeks gestation with hypoplastic left heart syndrome and intact or highly restrictive atrial septum underwent attempted prenatal intervention. under ultrasound guidance, the atrial septum was approached with a needle introduced percutaneously from the maternal abdominal surface. in 6 of 7 fetuses, the atrial septum was successfully perforated, with balloon dilation of this iatrogenic defect resulting in a small but persistent interatrial communication. there were no maternal complications. one fetus died after the procedure. the remaining fetuses were liveborn at term, although 4 died as neonates. conclusions ultrasound-guided fetal atrial septoplasty consisting of septal puncture and balloon dilation is feasible and can be performed percutaneously to minimize maternal risk. although we have not demonstrated any positive clinical impact to date, it is our hope that further technical evolution will ultimately enable prenatal left atrial decompression and improvement of outcomes in fetuses with hypoplastic left heart syndrome and intact atrial septum.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Clinical Medicine > Surgery > Cardiovascular Surgery

title: effect of patient-controlled perineural analgesia on rehabilitation and pain after ambulatory orthopedic surgery
display_name: Effect of Patient-controlled Perineural Analgesia on Rehabilitation and Pain after Ambulatory Orthopedic Surgery
abstract: background efficacy of continuous perineural and patient-controlled ropivacaine infusion at home after orthopedic surgery was compared with patient-controlled intravenous morphine for functional recovery and postoperative analgesia in a multicenter randomized trial. methods eighty-three patients scheduled to undergo acromioplasty or hallux valgus surgery received an interscalene (n = 40) or popliteal (n = 43) peripheral nerve block with 30 ml ropivacaine, 0.5%. after randomization, patients were discharged home 24 h after surgery with a disposable infusion pump delivering either patient-controlled intravenous morphine (n = 23) or perineural 0.2% ropivacaine infusion, either continuous infusion without bolus (n = 30) or basal infusion plus bolus (n = 30). the patients recorded pain scores on movement and/or walking and were directed to take paracetamol and rescue analgesics if necessary. the time necessary to be able to walk for 10 min; daily activities on days 1, 2, and 3; adverse events; and overall satisfaction scores were noted and graded by the patient. results basal-bolus ropivacaine decreased the time to 10 minutes' walk, optimized daily activities (p < 0.01), and decreased the amount of ropivacaine used. the morphine group had greater pain scores and consumption of morphine and ketoprofen compared with both ropivacaine groups (p < 0.05). the incidence of nausea/vomiting, sleep disturbance, and dizziness increased, and the patient satisfaction score decreased in the morphine group (p < 0.05). conclusions after ambulatory orthopedic surgery, 0.2% ropivacaine delivered as a perineural infusion using a disposable elastomeric pump with patient-controlled anesthesia bolus doses optimizes functional recovery and pain relief while decreasing the consumption of rescue analgesics and ropivacaine, and the number of adverse events.

title: clinical efficacy and safety of dexmedetomidine used as a preanesthetic prior to general anesthesia in cats
display_name: Clinical efficacy and safety of dexmedetomidine used as a preanesthetic prior to general anesthesia in cats
abstract: abstract objective to evaluate the clinical efficacy of dexmedetomidine as a preanesthetic medication administered prior to anesthetic induction with ketamine or propofol and with or without isoflurane for maintenance of anesthesia. design randomized, blinded, controlled clinical trial. animals 184 client-owned cats. procedures cats requiring general anesthesia for short or long procedures were assigned to receive 1 of 4 preanesthetic and induction drug combinations (dexmedetomidine and ketamine, placebo [saline {0.9% nacl} solution] and ketamine, dexmedetomidine and propofol, or placebo and propofol). cats undergoing long procedures received isoflurane for maintenance of anesthesia. results administration of dexmedetomidine prior to anesthetic induction with ketamine significantly increased the intubation success rate (57/64 [89%]), compared with the success rate for the placebo (4/37 [11 %]); significantly reduced the median induction dose of propofol ( 5.1 mg/kg [2.32 mg/lb]), compared with that for the placebo ( 10.5 mg/kg [4.77 mg/lb]); and significantly reduced the isoflurane concentration (1.5%) required for anesthesia maintenance, compared with that for the placebo (3.0%). postoperatively, fewer cats receiving dexmedetomidine required rescue analgesia, and cats had lower pain scores for at least 2 hours after surgery, compared with results for cats receiving the placebo. heart rate was lower during the procedure and respiratory rate and rectal temperature were lower during and after the procedure for cats receiving dexmedetomidine. more cats that received dexmedetomidine had emesis and pale mucous membranes, compared with the number of cats with those signs that received placebo. conclusions and clinical relevance dexmedetomidine as a preanesthetic was efficacious for clinical use in cats requiring general anesthesia.

title: bronchoscopic debulking of tracheal carcinoma in 3 cats using a wire snare
display_name: Bronchoscopic Debulking of Tracheal Carcinoma in 3 Cats using a Wire Snare
abstract: case 1: a 10-year-old spayed female domestic short-haired cat was presented to the university of california veterinary medical teaching hospital (ucd vmth) for a 1-month history of persistent respiratory difficulty that was nonresponsive to prednisolone and furosemide prescribed by the local veterinarian. on physical examination, the cat was quiet and alert with a body condition score of 8/9. the cat sat with elbows abducted and demonstrated marked abdominal effort on both inspiration and expiration. high-pitched stridor was auscultated over the trachea and referred airway sounds were heard over all of the thorax. the remainder of the physical examination was within normal limits. cervical and thoracic radiographs identified an intratracheal soft tissue mass at the level of the third rib. the remainder of thoracic radiographs were considered within normal limits, and an abdominal ultrasound examination with hepatic and splenic aspirates were unremarkable. the cat was anesthetized and tracheoscopy performed with a 5 mm 55 cm fiberoptic endoscope.a a broad-based tracheal mass was noted 3 cm proximal to the carina and occluded approximately 90% of the airway lumen (fig 1). multiple biopsy samples were collected with spiked-cup biopsy forcepsb and airway hemorrhage was controlled by intermittent suction. the obstruction was too far distal to bypass by a tracheostomy, and because of concerns about anesthetic recovery, attempts were made to debulk the mass. additional biopsy samples were obtained around the base of the obstruction to undermine the mass. a 1.8 mm 2-wire snareb was passed through the 2 mm biopsy channel of the endoscope, and the snare was twisted toward the wall of the trachea to encircle and entrap the mass. the instrument was retracted into the endoscope to sever the neoplasm from the tracheal wall, and the endoscope was withdrawn with the mass attached to the snare. using this approach, tracheal luminal diameter was restored to approximately 95% of normal (fig 2). bronchoscopy was completed with a 3.8 mm 55 cm video-endoscopec and identified a second mass occluding approximately 60% of a bronchial opening in the right caudal lung lobe (fig 3) and this mass was removed with spiked-cup biopsy forceps.b histopathology of both masses was consistent with a diagnosis of well-differentiated mucinous adenocarcinoma. bronchoscopic image of a tracheal carcinoma in cat 1. bronchoscopic view of the trachea after the tracheal carcinoma had been debulked and hemorrhage had been suctioned from the airway in cat 1. bronchoscopic image of a carcinoma identified in the right caudal lobar bronchus of cat 1. immediate improvement in respiratory effort was noted on the morning after the procedure. at 2-month re-evaluation, the cat was eupneic with a respiratory rate of 40 breaths/min. cervicothoracic radiographs disclosed mild thickening within the trachea at the site of mass removal. five months later, increased sounds were noted over the trachea on inspiration and expiration, and a high-pitched whistling sound was detected over the trachea on expiration. radiographs identified regrowth of the mass at the site of prior removal with occlusion of approximately one third of the tracheal luminal diameter. six months after the mass was debulked, increasing respiratory effort was noted. repeat endoscopy or placement of an intratracheal stent was declined, and the cat was euthanized. no necropsy was performed. case 2: a 16-year-old castrated male domestic medium-haired cat was presented to the ucd vmth with a 7-week history of wheezing and labored breathing that was nonresponsive to prednisone or amoxicillin-clavulanic acid.d on physical examination, there was marked abdominal effort on inspiration and expiration. increased breath sounds were auscultated over the extrathoracic trachea and all lung fields. cervical radiographs showed a narrowing of the trachea in the extrathoracic region compatible with an intramural tracheal lesion. ultrasound examination showed a mass within the tracheal wall. the cat was premedicated with oxymorphone, and induced and maintained on isoflurane with oxygen support provided by jet ventilation. tracheoscopy was performed with a 5 mm 55 cm fiberoptic endoscope.a a proliferative, broad-based lobular mass was evident approximately 3 cm distal to the larynx and extending 2 cm down the trachea. the mass appeared to encompass 7 8 tracheal rings. the mass was biopsied multiple times with the endoscopic cup biopsy forceps followed by removal of approximately 80% of the mass lesion with the endoscopic wire snare as described for case 1 (fig 4). minimal bleeding occurred and was controlled with suction. histopathology was consistent with a tracheal squamous cell carcinoma. respiration was improved after the procedure, and the cat was discharged. the cat, however, was euthanized 4 6 weeks after discharge for worsening respiratory distress, and no necropsy was performed. the endotracheal squamous cell carcinoma was entrapped by the wire snare and removed from cat 2. image was taken at withdrawal from the larynx. case 3: a 6-year-old spayed female egyptian mau cat presented for evaluation of inspiratory respiratory difficulty. physical examination disclosed inspiratory stridor, and cervical and thoracic radiographs indicated an intraluminal mass in the distal cervical trachea. the cat was anesthetized and supported with jet ventilation during tracheoscopy with a 5 mm 55 cm flexible fiberoptic endoscope.a a 2.5 3 cm broad-based mass was identified at the thoracic inlet and obstructed approximately 75% of the tracheal lumen. multiple biopsy samples were obtained with cup biopsy forceps to debulk the mass, and the cat was recovered from anesthesia. histopathology was consistent with adenocarcinoma. five weeks later, the cat was eupneic with a respiratory rate of 44 breaths/min and normal upper airway auscultation. computed tomography of the cervical region identified a sessile mass involving 50% of the tracheal circumference just cranial to the thoracic inlet. a ventral midline surgical approach was used to isolate the trachea and 8 tracheal rings were resected. an infiltrative adenocarcinoma was documented with neoplastic cells extending to the surgical margins. the owners declined follow-up radiation therapy. twenty-six months later, the cat represented for increased respiratory noises. stridor was present on physical examination, and cervical radiographs confirmed recurrence of the tracheal mass at the level of the thoracic inlet where the resection and anastomosis had been performed (fig 5). the cat was anesthetized and supported with jet ventilation for tracheoscopic debulking of the mass. tracheoscopy was performed with a 5 mm 55 cm fiberoptic endoscope,a and the mass was debulked with biopsy forceps and the wire snare as described for case 1. at re-evaluation 1 month later, mild end inspiratory stridor was auscultated. results of cervical radiographs were similar to those taken immediately after debulking. phone conversation with the owner 3 months later indicated that the cat was stable. nine months after tracheoscopic debulking of the neoplasm and 35 months after the initial diagnosis, the cat developed acute respiratory distress and was euthanized by the local veterinarian. no necropsy was performed. lateral neck radiograph from cat 3 showing a broad based mass within the tracheal lumen at the level of the thoracic inlet. tracheal neoplasia is uncommon in the cat, with lymphoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and adenocarcinoma reported most frequently.1 clinical signs often are indicative of airway obstruction, with respiratory difficulty reported most commonly. coughing, loud breathing, and dysphagia also can be seen. standard care for lymphoma includes chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or a combination of these, and long-term control of clinical signs has been reported.2 optimal treatment for other types of tracheal malignancies in human medicine involves resection and anastomosis,3 and this likely would be true for cats also. a review of all cases of tracheal neoplasia in cats seen at the ucd vmth over the time period from 2004 to 2009 identified 6 cases, with adenocarcinoma (n=3) diagnosed most commonly. the remaining 3 cats had carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and plasmacytoma. one cat with adenocarcinoma was treated with tracheal resection and anastomosis but was euthanized 4 days postoperatively after suffering cardiac arrest twice and being placed on a ventilator. the cat with complex carcinoma had obstruction of the left mainstem bronchus and collapse of left lung lobes, and was lost to follow-up after the diagnosis was made. the cat with plasmacytoma was treated with melphalan and steroids and was euthanized after 6 weeks because of worsening respiratory difficulty. interestingly, no reports of tracheal lymphoma were identified in our hospital population of cats over the aforementioned time period. there is a paucity of information on the comparative response and survival times of cats with tracheal neoplasms. a retrospective study evaluating outcome in 27 cats with both benign inflammatory and neoplastic laryngeal, laryngotracheal, and tracheal masses reported a median survival time of 5 days (range, 1 370 days) for cats with inflammatory obstructive masses, and 15.5 days (range, 1 1,109 days) for cats with neoplastic masses.1 therapies used in this group of cats ranged from none to single or multimodal therapy including medical and surgical options, and responses for tumors at all sites were grouped together. it is likely that optimal therapy for nonlymphomatous tracheal neoplasia is resection and anastomosis, but the extent and location of the tracheal neoplasm dictates whether it will be amenable to surgical resection and anastomosis. preoperative computed tomography with contrast is optimal to determine the extent of disease and screen the thorax for metastasis. preparation should be made for immediate surgical intervention or bronchoscopic debulking of the mass at the time of initial diagnostic evaluation because of the difficulty in recovering cats from anesthesia when airway obstruction is present. in addition, the tumor may be too distal in the airway to bypass with a tracheostomy, and tracheostomies are difficult to manage in cats.4 intrathoracic tracheal neoplasms require a more invasive surgical approach than do neoplasms located in the cervical region with the potential for substantial surgical and postoperative morbidity and mortality. in the cats described here, tracheal obstruction occurred in the distal cervical or intrathoracic region in each case, and bronchoscopic reduction of the mass prevented the need for thoracotomy. in our case series, all 3 intratracheal neoplasms were debulked by undermining the mass at its base with biopsy forceps, and then entrapping the mass with the 2-wire snare to sever it from its attachment to the tracheal wall. in the cats reported here, this technique markedly increased tracheal diameter and resulted in substantial improvement in clinical signs. this technique is similar to that described for safe and effective treatment of humans with benign tracheal masses, where a laser is used to undermine the mass followed by removal with an endoscopic snare.5 removal of a mass by laser or electrocautery would likely be an effective technique in the cat and would have the benefit of controlling airway hemorrhage, although access to appropriate equipment could limit implementation of this methodology. in the dog, bronchoscopic reduction of a mass obstructing the right mainstem bronchus has been described, but the dog lived only 1 month after the procedure.6 importantly, cats treated in this manner had prolonged survival without need for continued medical therapy. the cat with the shortest survival time (case 2) was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma rather than adenocarcinoma, but it is not possible to generalize regarding response to therapy with such a small case series. interestingly, the cat with the longest survival time (9 months) had previously undergone tracheal resection and anastomosis that was followed by bronchoscopic debulking when the mass recurred. this finding suggests that substantial palliation of signs can be achieved when a slow-growing tumor is removed by debulking and surgical therapy is not an option. another palliative option considered in case 1 to manage regrowth of the intratracheal neoplasm was placement of an intraluminal tracheal stent, either alone or after debulking of the mass. stent placement has successfully palliated signs of airway obstruction in cats with benign and malignant tracheal lesions, but metastatic disease resulted in euthanasia 6 weeks after stent placement in the sole cat with malignancy.7 interestingly, case 1 reported here had metastatic disease at the time of removal of the tracheal lesion yet still survived 5 months with simple debulking of the obstructive mass within the trachea. bronchoscopic debulking of tracheal masses is a relatively simple, noninvasive, and safe means of palliating tracheal tumors in cats. major complications that could be encountered with bronchoscopic debulking include excessive hemorrhage and tracheal perforation. no clinically important complications were encountered in our case series, and none of the 3 cats required placement of a temporary tracheostomy tube. aolympus p20d, olympus corporation, melville, ny bolympus endoscopic instruments, olympus corporation colympus bf3c160, olympus corporation damoxicillin-clavulanic acid, pfizer animal health, new york, ny

title: influence of leukocyte- and platelet-rich fibrin (l-prf) in the healing of simple postextraction sockets: a split-mouth study
display_name: Influence of Leukocyte- and Platelet-Rich Fibrin (L-PRF) in the Healing of Simple Postextraction Sockets: A Split-Mouth Study
abstract: the aim of this study was to evaluate the effects of leukocyte- and platelet-rich fibrin (l-prf) on the pain and soft tissue healing after tooth extractions. twenty-six patients (9 males and 17 females) were treated with multiple extractions (2 to 8), with a total of 108 extractions. this was an exploratory single blinded randomized clinical trial with a split-mouth design. the pain after the surgery was assessed in each patient by the vas scale (1 to 10) at intervals of 24-48-72-96 hours. the soft tissue healing was clinically evaluated at 3, 7, 14, and 21 days after surgery by the same examiner surgeon, using the modified healing index (4 to 12). the mean value of postextraction pain was 3.2 0.3 in the experimental sides and 4.1 0.1 in the control sides. after 7 days from the extractions, the values of modified healing index in the experimental and control groups were, respectively, 4.8 0.6 and 5.1 0.9. the use of l-prf in postextraction sockets filling can be proposed as a useful procedure in order to manage the postoperative pain and to promote the soft tissue healing process, reducing the early adverse effects of the inflammation.

title: factors associated with prolonged length of stay following cardiac surgery in a major referral hospital in oman: a retrospective observational study
display_name: Factors associated with prolonged length of stay following cardiac surgery in a major referral hospital in Oman: a retrospective observational study
abstract: objectives two objectives were set for this study. the first was to identify factors influencing prolonged postoperative length of stay (los) following cardiac surgery. the second was to devise a predictive model for prolonged los in the cardiac intensive care unit (cicu) based on preoperative factors available at admission and to compare it against two existing cardiac stratification systems. design observational retrospective study. settings a tertiary hospital in oman. participants all adult patients who underwent cardiac surgery at a major referral hospital in oman between 2009 and 2013. results 30.5% of the patients had prolonged los ( 11 days) after surgery, while 17% experienced prolonged icu los ( 5 days). factors that were identified to prolong cicu los were non-elective surgery, current congestive heart failure (chf), renal failure, combined coronary artery bypass graft (cabg) and valve surgery, and other non-isolated valve or cabg surgery. patients were divided into three groups based on their scores. the probabilities of prolonged cicu los were 11%, 26% and 28% for group 1, 2 and 3, respectively. the predictive model had an area under the curve of 0.75. factors associated with prolonged overall postoperative los included the body mass index, the type of surgery, cardiopulmonary bypass machine use, packed red blood cells use, non-elective surgery and number of complications. the latter was the most important determinant of postoperative los. conclusions patient management can be tailored for individual patient based on their treatments and personal attributes to optimise resource allocation. moreover, a simple predictive score system to enable identification of patients at risk of prolonged cicu stay can be developed using data that are routinely collected by most hospitals.

title: leptin and the perioperative neuroendocrinological stress response 1
display_name: Leptin and the Perioperative Neuroendocrinological Stress Response<sup>1</sup>
abstract: the human response to surgical stress is characterized by massive release of neuroendocrine hormones, provoking catabolism, thermogenesis, and hyperglycemia. considering the possible adverse outcomes of excessive stress hormones, understanding various components of the stress response may improve management of postoperative morbidity. leptin, initially described as an adipocyte-derived signaling factor, may also play an important role in regulating the hypothalamo-pituitary-adrenocortical axis. in phase i, plasma leptin and cortisol were measured in women before, during, and after total abdominal hysterectomy. the anesthetic technique was strictly controlled, balanced anesthesia. in phase ii, plasma leptin and cortisol levels were measured in cardiac surgery patients. these subjects were anesthetized with a high dose opioid technique that blunts the intraoperative surgical stress response. in phase i, mean leptin levels did not change over the week before surgery, had a maximal decrease to 49% of baseline 2 h after surgery, and increased to just above baseline 24 h postoperatively. cortisol was 176% of the baseline just before surgery, peaked at 2 h after surgery (383%), and remained elevated 24 h (200%) and 48 h (165%) after surgery. during the first 2 h of surgery, the decrease in leptin parallels the increase in cortisol. in phase ii, high dose fentanyl limited both the cortisol increase and the leptin decrease; thus, the ratio of cortisol increase to leptin decrease was similar for the cardiac patients and the hysterectomy patients. these data indicate that leptin has a role in the surgically induced acute stress response in humans. early in surgery the decrease in leptin parallels the increase in cortisol. this suggests a possible relationship between the neurobiology of these two systems, which could have important implications for regulation of the neuroendocrine response to surgical stress.

title: the perioperative complication rate of orthopedic surgery in sickle cell disease: report of the national sickle cell surgery study group
display_name: The perioperative complication rate of orthopedic surgery in sickle cell disease: Report of the national sickle cell surgery study group
abstract: orthopedic disease affects the majority of sickle cell anemia patients of which aseptic necrosis of the hip is the most common, occurring in up to 50% of patients. we conducted a multicentered study to determine the perioperative complications among sickle cell patients assigned to different transfusion regimens prior to orthopedic procedures: 118 patients underwent 138 surgeries. the overall serious complication rate was 67%. the most common of these were excessive intraoperative blood loss, defined as in excess of 10% of blood volume. the next most common complication was sickle cell-related events (acute chest syndrome or vaso-occlusive crisis), which occurred in 17% of cases. while preoperative transfusion group assignment did not predict overall complication rates, higher risk procedures were associated with significantly higher rates of overall complications. transfusion complications were experienced by 12% of the patients. two patients died following surgery. both deaths were associated with an acute pulmonary event. the 52 patients undergoing hip replacements experienced the highest rate of complications with excessive intraoperative blood loss occurring in the majority of patients. sickle cell-related events occurred in 19% of patients, and surgical complications occurred after 15% of hip replacements and included postoperative hemorrhage, dislocated prosthesis, wound abscess, and rupture of the femoral prosthesis. there were twenty-two hip coring procedures. acute chest syndrome occurred in 14% of the patients. overall, decompression coring was a safer, shorter operation. a randomized prospective trial to determine the perioperative and long-term efficacy of core decompression for avascular necrosis of the hip in sickle cell disease is needed. in conclusion, this study demonstrates a high rate of perioperative complications despite compliance with sickle cell perioperative care guidelines. pulmonary complications and transfusion reactions were common. this study supports the results previously published by the national preoperative transfusion in sickle cell disease group. these results stated that a conservative preoperative transfusion regimen to bring hemoglobin concentration to between 9 and 11 g/dl was as effective as an aggressive transfusion regimen in which the hemoglobin s level was lowered to 30%.

abstract: background the current prevalence of hospital-acquired infections and evolving amplification of bacterial resistance are major public health concerns. a heightened awareness of intraoperative transmission of potentially pathogenic bacterial organisms may lead to implementation of effective preventative measures. methods sixty-one operative suites were randomly selected for analysis. sterile intravenous stopcock sets and two sites on the anesthesia machine were decontaminated and cultured aseptically at baseline and at case completion. the primary outcome was the presence of a positive culture on the previously sterile patient stopcock set. secondary outcomes were the number of colonies per surface area sampled on the anesthesia machine, species identification, and antibiotic susceptibility of isolated organisms. results bacterial contamination of the anesthesia work area increased significantly at the case conclusion, with a mean difference of 115 colonies per surface area sampled (95% confidence interval [ci], 62-169; p < 0.001). transmission of bacterial organisms, including vancomycin-resistant enterococcus, to intravenous stopcock sets occurred in 32% (95% ci, 20.6-44.9%) of cases. highly contaminated work areas increased the odds of stopcock contamination by 4.7 (95% ci, 1.42-15.42; p = 0.011). contaminated intravenous tubing was associated with a trend toward increased nosocomial infection rates (odds ratio, 3.08; 95% ci, 0.56-17.5; p = 0.11) and with an increase in mortality (95% ci odds ratio, 1.11-infinity; p = 0.0395). conclusion potentially pathogenic, multidrug-resistant bacterial organisms are transmitted during the practice of general anesthesia to both the anesthesia work area and intravenous stopcock sets. implementation of infection control measures in this area may help to reduce both the evolving problem of increasing bacterial resistance and the development of life-threatening infectious complications.

abstract: following cardiac valve replacement, new small ischemic brain lesions were detected by diffusion-weighted mri. neurocognitive decline was present early after operation, but resolved within 4 months. a correlation of new ischemic lesions to postoperative cognitive dysfunction or clinical variables was not found.

title: prediction of postoperative pulmonary complications in a population-based surgical cohort

authorships.name: Jaume Canet

authorships.name: Valentín Mazo
institutions: Hospital Universitari Germans Trias i Pujol

authorships.name: Z. Briones
institutions: Hospital Universitari Germans Trias i Pujol

abstract: background current knowledge of the risk for postoperative pulmonary complications (ppcs) rests on studies that narrowly selected patients and procedures. hypothesizing that ppc occurrence could be predicted from a reduced set of perioperative variables, we aimed to develop a predictive index for a broad surgical population. methods patients undergoing surgical procedures given general, neuraxial, or regional anesthesia in 59 hospitals were randomly selected for this prospective, multicenter study. the main outcome was the development of at least one of the following: respiratory infection, respiratory failure, bronchospasm, atelectasis, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, or aspiration pneumonitis. the cohort was randomly divided into a development subsample to construct a logistic regression model and a validation subsample. a ppc predictive index was constructed. results of 2,464 patients studied, 252 events were observed in 123 (5%). thirty-day mortality was higher in patients with a ppc (19.5%; 95% [ci], 12.5-26.5%) than in those without a ppc (0.5%; 95% ci, 0.2-0.8%). regression modeling identified seven independent risk factors: low preoperative arterial oxygen saturation, acute respiratory infection during the previous month, age, preoperative anemia, upper abdominal or intrathoracic surgery, surgical duration of at least 2 h, and emergency surgery. the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 90% (95% ci, 85-94%) for the development subsample and 88% (95% ci, 84-93%) for the validation subsample. conclusion the risk index based on seven objective, easily assessed factors has excellent discriminative ability. the index can be used to assess individual risk of ppc and focus further research on measures to improve patient care.

title: intrathecal and epidural anesthesia and analgesia for cardiac surgery
display_name: Intrathecal and Epidural Anesthesia and Analgesia for Cardiac Surgery
abstract: inadequate analgesia and/or an uninhibited stress response during the postoperative period may lead to many adverse hemodynamic, metabolic, immunologic, and hemostatic alterations [1-3]. aggressive control of postoperative pain with regional anesthesia and analgesia, associated with an attenuated stress response, may decrease morbidity and mortality in high-risk patients after noncardiac surgery [4,5]. aggressive control of postoperative pain with intravenous (iv) analgesics, associated with an attenuated stress response in patients after cardiac surgery, may also decrease morbidity and mortality [6,7]. the perioperative use of intrathecal (it) or epidural (epi) anesthesia and analgesia in patients undergoing cardiac surgery may beneficially affect outcome by producing intense postoperative analgesia, stress-response attenuation, and thoracic cardiac sympathectomy. however, the technique can be associated with undesirable drug effects that may possibly increase morbidity, and it entails an increased risk of hematoma formation. this review article summarizes the risks and benefits associated with the application of it and epi anesthesia and analgesia in patients undergoing cardiac surgery and suggests future directions for investigation. potential benefits in patients undergoing cardiac surgery, perioperative myocardial ischemia (diagnosed by electrocardiography and/or transesophageal echocardiography) is most commonly observed during the immediate postoperative period (25%-38% incidence) and is related to outcome [8,9]. intraoperatively, initiation of cardiopulmonary bypass (cpb) causes significant increases in stress-response hormones (norepinephrine, epinephrine, etc.) that persist into the immediate postoperative period and may contribute to myocardial ischemia observed during this time [10-12]. furthermore, postoperative myocardial ischemia may be aggravated by cardiac sympathetic nerve activation, which disrupts the balance between coronary blood flow and myocardial oxygen demand [13]. during the pivotal immediate postoperative period after cardiac surgery, the major potential benefits offered by it or epi anesthesia and analgesia are intense analgesia, stress-response attenuation, and thoracic cardiac sympathectomy. intense postoperative analgesia aggressive control of postoperative pain in patients after cardiac surgery may beneficially affect outcome. in adults undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting (cabg), intense analgesia (continuous iv sufentanil infusion) during the immediate postoperative period (first 18 h) decreases the incidence and severity of myocardial ischemia as diagnosed by electrocardiography [6]. in neonates undergoing cardiac surgery, intense analgesia (continuous iv fentanyl or sufentanil infusion) during the immediate postoperative period (first 24 h) decreases morbidity and mortality [7]. unfortunately, aggressive control of pain with iv opioids in this manner does not allow tracheal extubation to occur in the immediate postoperative period. it or epi anesthesia and analgesia are attractive alternatives to iv opioids in this setting for their potential to produce intense analgesia yet still allow extubation to occur in the immediate postoperative period. stress response attenuation an uninhibited stress response during the postoperative period may lead to many adverse hemodynamic (tachycardia, hypertension, vasoconstriction), metabolic (increased catabolism), immunologic (impaired immune response), and hemostatic (platelet activation) alterations [1-3]. it or epi anesthesia and analgesia (with local anesthetics or opioids) can effectively inhibit the stress response associated with surgical procedures [13]. local anesthetics appear to possess greater efficacy than opioids in stress-response attenuation, perhaps because of their unique mechanism of action [13]. although still a matter of some debate, stress-response attenuation with epi local anesthetics and/or opioids in high-risk patients after major noncardiac surgery may decrease morbidity and mortality [4,5,13]. in patients undergoing cardiac surgery, initiation of cpb causes significant increases in stress-response hormones that persist into the immediate postoperative period [10-12]. attenuation of this component of the stress response with iv opioids may also decrease morbidity and mortality [6,7]. unfortunately, stress-response attenuation in patients undergoing cardiac surgery with iv opioids in this manner does not allow extubation to occur in the immediate postoperative period. it or epi anesthesia and analgesia (particularly with local anesthetics) are attractive alternatives to iv opioids in this setting for their potential to attenuate the stress response yet still allow extubation to occur in the immediate postoperative period. thoracic cardiac sympathectomy the myocardium and coronary vasculature are densely innervated by sympathetic nerve fibers that arise from t1 to t5 and profoundly influence total coronary blood flow and distribution [14]. cardiac sympathetic nerve activation initiates coronary artery vasoconstriction [15] and paradoxical vasoconstriction in response to intrinsic vasodilators [16]. in patients with coronary artery disease, cardiac sympathetic nerve activation disrupts the normal matching of coronary blood flow and myocardial oxygen demand [17,18]. animal models show an intense poststenotic vasoconstrictive mechanism mediated by cardiac sympathetic nerve activation that attenuates local metabolic vasodilation in response to myocardial ischemia [19,20]. furthermore, myocardial ischemia initiates a cardiocardiac reflex mediated by sympathetic nerve fibers, which augments the ischemic process [21]. cardiac sympathetic nerve activation likely plays a central role in initiating postoperative myocardial ischemia by decreasing the myocardial oxygen supply via the mechanisms listed above [13,22]. thoracic epi anesthesia with local anesthetics effectively blocks cardiac sympathetic nerve afferent and efferent fibers [13]. opioids, which are administered similarly, are unable to effectively block cardiac sympathetic nerve activity [13]. patients with symptomatic coronary artery disease benefit from cardiac sympathectomy, and the application of thoracic sympathetic blockade in the management of angina pectoris was described as early as 1965 [23]. thoracic epi anesthesia with local anesthetics increases the diameter of stenotic epicardial coronary artery segments without causing dilation of coronary arterioles [17], decreases determinants of myocardial oxygen demand [18], improves left ventricular function [24], and decreases anginal symptoms [25,26]. furthermore, cardiac sympathectomy increases the endocardial to epicardial blood flow ratio [27,28], beneficially affects collateral blood flow during myocardial ischemia [28], decreases poststenotic vasoconstriction [20], and attenuates the myocardial ischemia-induced cardiocardiac reflex [20]. in an animal model, thoracic epi anesthesia with local anesthetics decreased myocardial infarct size after coronary artery occlusion [27]. of note, these beneficial effects are not caused by systemic absorption of the local anesthetic [27]. in short, thoracic epi anesthesia with local anesthetics may benefit patients undergoing cardiac surgery by effectively blocking cardiac sympathetic nerve activity and improving the myocardial oxygen supply-demand balance. clinical utilization (table 1 and table 2) summarize investigations detailing the application of it [29-42]1 and epi [43-58] anesthesia and analgesia to patients undergoing cardiac surgery.table 1: reports of intrathecal anesthesia and analgesia for cardiac surgerytable 2: reports of epidural anesthesia and analgesia for cardiac surgery(1) vincenty c, malone b, mathru m, venus b. comparison of intrathecal and intravenous morphine in post coronary bypass surgery [abstract]. crit care med 1985;13:308. intrathecal anesthesia and analgesia application of it analgesia to patients undergoing cardiac surgery was initially reported by mathews and abrams in 1980 [42]. they described the administration of it morphine (1.5-4.0 mg) to 40 adults after the induction of anesthesia for cardiac surgery [42]. postoperatively, all 40 patients were entirely pain free for the first 27.5 h, and 17 did not require any analgesics prior to discharge from the hospital [42]. of the 17 patients who received 4.0 mg of it morphine, 11 required no postoperative analgesic drugs [42]. after this impressive display, others have subsequently applied it anesthesia and analgesia to patients undergoing cardiac surgery (table 1). most have used it morphine in hopes of providing prolonged postoperative analgesia. some have used it fentanyl, sufentanil, or local anesthetics for intraoperative anesthesia and analgesia (with stress response attenuation) and/or thoracic cardiac sympathectomy. two randomized, blind, placebo-controlled studies demonstrate the ability of it morphine to induce significant postoperative analgesia after cardiac surgery. in the first study, patients were randomized to receive either it morphine (4.0 mg) or it placebo prior to the induction of anesthesia [30]. intraoperative anesthetic management was standardized, and after tracheal extubation, all received exclusively iv morphine via patient-controlled analgesia [30]. patients who received it morphine required significantly less iv morphine than placebo controls (33.2 vs 51.1 mg, respectively) during the initial 48 postoperative hours [30]. in the second study, patients were randomized to receive either it morphine (0.5 mg) or it placebo prior to the induction of anesthesia [37]. intraoperative anesthetic management was standardized and, postoperatively, all patients received exclusively iv morphine administered by a nurse who tried to keep the linear analog pain score at less than 4 (a score of 1 represented no pain, 10 represented the worst pain imaginable; the scale was 25 cm long) [37]. patients who received it morphine required significantly less iv morphine than placebo controls (2.4 vs 8.3 mg, respectively) during the initial 30 h after it injection [37]. many fewer well designed studies (retrospective, observational, etc.) attest to the ability of it morphine to induce substantial postoperative analgesia in patients after cardiac surgery (table 1). doses of 0.5-10.0 mg administered prior to cpb initiate reliable postoperative analgesia, the quality of which depends not only on the dose administered but also on the type and amount of iv analgesics used for the intraoperative baseline anesthetic. the optimal dose of it morphine for achieving the maximum postoperative analgesia with minimum undesirable drug effects is uncertain. naturally, when larger doses of it morphine are used, more intense and prolonged postoperative analgesia is purchased at the expense of more undesirable drug effects [36,41]. because of morphine's low lipid solubility, analgesic effects after it injection are delayed. thus, even large doses of it morphine administered to patients before cardiac surgery do not initiate reliable intraoperative analgesia [37-39,41] and therefore would not be expected to attenuate the stress response associated with cpb. only an extremely large dose of it morphine (10.0 mg) may initiate reliable intraoperative analgesia in this setting.1 only one study has examined the ability of it morphine to attenuate the stress response associated with cpb as measured by blood catecholamine levels [30]. patients were randomized to receive either it morphine (4.0 mg) or it placebo prior to the induction of anesthesia [30]. intraoperative anesthetic management was standardized, and arterial blood samples were obtained perioperatively to ascertain norepinephrine and epinephrine levels [30]. patients who were administered it morphine experienced similar perioperative increases in blood catecholamine levels when compared with placebo controls [30]. although unable to attenuate the stress response associated with cpb, it morphine (by initiating postoperative analgesia) may attenuate the stress response during the immediate postoperative period [37]. patients who were administered 0.5 mg of it morphine prior to the induction of anesthesia not only required significantly less iv morphine postoperatively than placebo controls but also required significantly less iv nitroprusside (58.1 vs 89.1 mg, respectively) during the initial 24 postoperative hours to control hypertension, which suggests partial stress response attenuation [37]. some investigators have used it fentanyl, sufentanil, or local anesthetics, hoping to provide intraoperative anesthesia and analgesia (and stress-response attenuation), with mixed results (table 1). administration of it local anesthetics to patients after the induction of anesthesia for cardiac surgery may help promote intraoperative hemodynamic stability [31,33], whereas it sufentanil (50 micro g), administered prior to the induction of anesthesia for cardiac surgery can reduce volatile anesthetic requirements during mediastinal dissection but is unable to reliably block hemodynamic responses to laryngoscopy and intubation [34]. most attempts at inducing thoracic cardiac sympathectomy in patients undergoing cardiac surgery have utilized thoracic epi anesthesia with local anesthetics. only one group of investigators has attempted cardiac sympathectomy in this setting with an it injection of local anesthetics. as reviewed retrospectively, 18 adult patients were administered lumbar it hyperbaric bupivacaine (23-30 mg) and/or hyperbaric lidocaine (150 mg) mixed with morphine (0.5-1.0 mg) after the induction of anesthesia [33]. in an attempt to produce a total spinal and, thus, thoracic cardiac sympathectomy, trendelenburg position was maintained for at least 10 min after the it injection [33]. heart rate decreased significantly (baseline mean 67 bpm to postinjection mean 52 bpm) after injection (indicating cardiac sympathectomy was obtained), and no patient exhibited electrocardiographic evidence of myocardial ischemia prior to cpb [33]. although the authors report that the technique provided stable perioperative hemodynamics, 17 of 18 patients required iv phenylephrine at some time intraoperatively to increase blood pressure [33]. the same group reports similar hemodynamic changes that occurred in a 10-yr-old child with kawasaki disease who underwent cabg after receiving it hyperbaric bupivacaine mixed with morphine via a lumbar puncture after induction of anesthesia [31]. in summary, the administration of it morphine to patients prior to cpb initiates reliable postoperative analgesia after cardiac surgery. it opioids or local anesthetics cannot reliably attenuate the stress response associated with cpb that persists during the immediate postoperative period. although it local anesthetics (not opioids) may induce thoracic cardiac sympathectomy, the hemodynamic changes associated with a total spinal make the technique unpalatable. epidural anesthesia and analgesia application of epi anesthesia and analgesia to patients undergoing cardiac surgery was initially reported by hoar et al. in 1976 [58]. they described the intraoperative insertion of thoracic epi catheters in 12 patients after cabg. the catheters were injected with lidocaine and bupivacaine during the postoperative period to promote analgesia and control hypertension [58]. the 1987 article by el-baz and goldin [56] was the first to report the insertion of thoracic epi catheters in patients prior to initiation of cardiac surgery. others have subsequently applied epi anesthesia and analgesia to patients undergoing cardiac surgery (table 2). most have used epi local anesthetics in hopes of providing stress-response attenuation and/or thoracic cardiac sympathectomy. some have used epi opioids to provide intraoperative and/or postoperative analgesia. epi anesthesia and analgesia with local anesthetics and/or opioids induce significant postoperative analgesia in patients after cardiac surgery. patients randomized to receive a continuous thoracic epi morphine infusion (0.1 mg/h) after cardiac surgery required significantly less supplemental iv morphine than patients without epi catheters (5 vs 18 mg/day per patient, respectively) during the initial 3 postoperative days [56]. children (aged 2-12 yr) randomized to receive caudal epi morphine (75 micro g/kg) intraoperatively after cardiac surgery required significantly less supplemental iv morphine than patients who did not receive epi morphine (0.32 vs 0.71 mg/kg, respectively) during the initial 24 postoperative hours [54]. other studies further attest to the ability of epi anesthesia and analgesia with local anesthetics and/or opioids to induce substantial postoperative analgesia in patients after cardiac surgery [43,50,52,55,57,58]. epi anesthesia with local anesthetics significantly attenuates the stress response in patients undergoing cardiac surgery. patients randomized to receive intermittent boluses of thoracic epi bupivacaine intraoperatively followed by continuous infusion postoperatively exhibited significantly decreased blood levels of norepinephrine and epinephrine perioperatively when compared with patients managed similarly without epi catheters [49]. furthermore, increased blood catecholamine levels in these patients were associated with increased systemic vascular resistance [49]. patients randomized to receive a continuous thoracic epi bupivacaine infusion perioperatively exhibited significantly decreased blood levels of norepinephrine and cortisol perioperatively when compared with patients managed similarly without epi catheters [45]. patients randomized to receive a continuous thoracic epi bupivacaine and sufentanil infusion perioperatively exhibited significantly decreased blood levels of norepinephrine after sternotomy when compared with patients managed similarly without epi catheters [53]. other studies further attest to the ability of epi anesthesia with local anesthetics to promote perioperative hemodynamic stability in patients undergoing cardiac surgery, which suggests stress-response attenuation [47,48,51,58]. one study indicates that epi analgesia with opioids significantly attenuates the stress response in patients undergoing cardiac surgery [56]. patients randomized to receive a continuous thoracic epi morphine infusion postoperatively exhibited significantly decreased blood levels of cortisol and beta-endorphin postoperatively when compared with patients managed similarly without epi catheters [56]. two provocative studies demonstrate the ability of epi anesthesia to induce significant thoracic cardiac sympathectomy in patients undergoing cardiac surgery. in the first study, patients undergoing cabg were evaluated with reverse thermodilution catheters that had been placed in the mid-coronary sinus under fluoroscopic guidance prior to the induction of anesthesia [46]. intraoperative anesthetic management was standardized. coronary sinus blood flow was measured by a constant infusion technique, and coronary vascular resistance was calculated utilizing coronary perfusion pressure (arterial diastolic pressure minus pulmonary capillary wedge pressure) and coronary sinus blood flow [46]. patients who had been randomized to receive intermittent boluses of thoracic epi bupivacaine intraoperatively followed by continuous infusion postoperatively exhibited significant decreases in coronary vascular resistance post-cpb when compared with pre-cpb values, whereas patients managed similarly without epi catheters exhibited significant increases in coronary vascular resistance post-cpb [46]. in the second study, patients undergoing cabg were evaluated with catheters that had been placed in the coronary sinus under fluoroscopic guidance and continuous pressure monitoring prior to the induction of anesthesia [47]. intraoperative anesthetic management was standardized, and all patients received a continuous iv infusion of tritiated norepinephrine [47]. to assess cardiac sympathetic activity, blood samples were obtained from the coronary sinus and radial artery, and the rate of norepinephrine spillover from the heart was calculated according to the fick principle [47]. patients randomized to receive a single bolus of thoracic epi mepivacaine immediately after the induction of anesthesia exhibited significantly decreased cardiac norepinephrine spillover after sternotomy when compared with patients managed similarly without epi catheters [47]. furthermore, 20% of patients managed without epi catheters exhibited electrocardiographic evidence of myocardial ischemia after sternotomy, whereas no patient managed with an epi catheter exhibited myocardial ischemia during this time [47]. perioperative cardiac sympathectomy induced via thoracic epi anesthesia with local anesthetics may benefit patients undergoing cardiac surgery by increasing the myocardial oxygen supply [17,27,28]. however, such a cardiac sympathectomy offers additional benefits to patients undergoing cardiac surgery. multiple studies demonstrate that epi anesthesia with local anesthetics significantly decreases heart rate before [51] and after [45,52] cpb and significantly decreases the need to administer beta-blockers after cpb [48]. multiple studies also demonstrate that epi anesthesia with local anesthetics significantly decreases systemic vascular resistance before [47,49] and after [52,55] cpb. furthermore, patients undergoing cardiac surgery who received thoracic epidural anesthesia with local anesthetics not only exhibited significant decreases in postoperative heart rate and systemic vascular resistance but also exhibited significant decreases in postoperative electrocardiographic evidence of myocardial ischemia when compared with patients managed similarly without epi catheters [52]. in summary, administration of epi opioids or local anesthetics to patients before and/or after cpb initiates reliable postoperative analgesia after cardiac surgery. administration of epi local anesthetics (not opioids) can both reliably attenuate the stress response associated with cpb that persists during the immediate postoperative period and induce thoracic cardiac sympathectomy. clinical outcome all reports of it and epi anesthesia and analgesia for cardiac surgery involve small numbers of patients, and few are well designed (table 1 and table 2). only four studies involving it analgesia are prospective, randomized, blind, and placebo-controlled, whereas there are no blind, placebo-controlled studies involving epi anesthesia and analgesia. furthermore, none of the studies involving it and epi anesthesia and analgesia for cardiac surgery use clinical outcome as a primary end point. thus, there are clear deficiencies in the literature that prohibit definitive analysis of the risk-benefit ratio of it and epi anesthesia and analgesia for cardiac surgery. undesirable drug effects opioids although title: thoracic epidural anesthesia as the last option for treating angina in a patient before coronary artery bypass surgery
display_name: Thoracic Epidural Anesthesia as the Last Option for Treating Angina in a Patient Before Coronary Artery Bypass Surgery
abstract: ischemic cardiomyopathy in a patient with medically refractory unstable angina is a difficult clinical scenario. unfavorable anatomy and/or comorbidity can prohibit the safe performance of angioplasty or coronary artery bypass (cab) surgery. thoracic epidural anesthesia (tea) has been used successfully to stabilize patients with unstable angina refractory to maximum medical therapy [1]. tea has also been used during and after cab surgery in patients with preserved left ventricular function [2,3]. we describe a patient with intractable angina, poor ventricular function, and complicated comorbidities who received tea for angina, later underwent cab surgery using tea in combination with general anesthesia, and continued to receive tea for postoperative pain relief. case report a 68-yr-old man was transferred from another hospital with persistent angina at rest 4 days after a non-q wave myocardial infarction. the patient had been treated with heparin, nitroglycerin, morphine, and metoprolol intravenously (iv) and aspirin by mouth without improvement from his anginal symptoms. his comorbidities included hypertension, peripheral vascular disease, a prior cerebrovascular accident with left-sided weakness, prior dual-chamber paced, dual-chamber sensed, dual-chamber response pacemaker implantation for complete heart block, hematuria, and acute tubular necrosis superimposed on chronic renal insufficiency. the patient underwent cardiac catheterization on admission, during which his blood pressure was 74/48 mm hg, and his pulmonary capillary wedge pressure was 20 mm hg. his electrocardiogram showed atrial and ventricular pacing at 80 bpm. coronary angiography revealed a proximal 95% stenosis of the left anterior descending artery, a total occlusion of the circumflex artery at its midpoint with collateral filling by obtuse marginal branches, and a 40% occlusion of the right coronary artery. transthoracic echocardiography showed global hypokinesis, anteroseptal dyskinesis, and inferior akinesis. his ejection fraction (ef) by multiple-uptake gated acquisition scan was 20%, and a resting thallium scintigraphy scan showed redistribution in the anterior and anteroseptal walls. his chest radiograph was significant for mild pulmonary edema. abnormal laboratory values included a serum creatinine level of 5.7 mg/dl, a blood urea nitrogen level of 39 mg/dl, and red blood cells on urinalysis. the cardiac surgical service was consulted to consider cab surgery. the operative risk was deemed prohibitively high and medical therapy was maximized with iv morphine, nitroglycerin, heparin, and atenolol, and with the use of intraaortic balloon pump counterpulsation. the patient's blood pressure improved to 98/60 mm hg and remained stable over the next 3 days. however, his angina persisted, suggesting ongoing ischemia, and tea was offered as a last therapeutic option. the patient was weaned from intraaortic balloon pump support, and the heparin infusion was stopped without a change in the patient's hemodynamic parameters or symptoms. six hours after discontinuing the heparin infusion, an epidural catheter was placed at the t2-t3 level with the patient in the lateral decubitus position. the epidural space was identified via the midline approach and the catheter's position confirmed by the outline of a bolus of radioopaque dye into the epidural space. the catheter was tunneled for 6 cm under the skin to protect against displacement and lessen the chance of infection. following catheter placement, a 5-ml bolus of 0.25% bupivacaine completely relieved the patient's angina. arterial blood pressure and heart rate remained unchanged and iv nitrates and morphine were discontinued. because the patient's angina recurred in between epidural catheter boluses, an infusion of 0.0625% bupivacaine with 100 micro g/ml of morphine was started at 4 ml/h. during the following 15 days, the patient remained pain free except on two occasions, in which "breakthrough" pain was treated with a bolus of 5 ml of 0.25% bupivacaine. myocardial enzyme panels drawn after the episodes of breakthrough pain were within normal limits. two weeks after admission, the acute tubular necrosis and hematuria had resolved and he was able to ambulate without pain. four-vessel cab surgery, with intraoperative and postoperative tea, was planned for day 16 of his admission. after induction of general anesthesia, an epidural infusion of 0.5% bupivacaine with 100 micro g/ml of morphine at 5 ml/h was started, supplemented by iv boluses of sufentanil and midazolam. the patient separated from cardiopulmonary bypass with 0.025 micro g [center dot] kg-1 [center dot] min-1 of epinephrine and 50 micro g/min of nitroglycerin. hemodynamic parameters prebypass, during bypass, and postbypass were stable. on arrival in the intensive care unit, the concentration of bupivacaine was halved. the patient was tracheally extubated 18 h postoperatively. on postoperative day 2, the bupivacaine concentration was halved again to 0.125% and continued until postoperative day 5. the patient did not use any iv opioids postoperatively. he was discharged from the hospital 8 days after surgery. discussion we describe a patient in whom tea was the last therapeutic option available for stabilization prior to cab surgery. tea was continued with excellent intraoperative and postoperative clinical outcomes. angina is mediated via sympathetic afferent nerve fibers, and thus a tea-induced sympathectomy can be used to effectively treat this manifestation of myocardial ischemia [4,5]. there is concern that tea may alleviate chest pain but mask ongoing myocardial ischemia. however, numerous animal and human studies have demonstrated the beneficial effects of tea on the determinants of myocardial ischemia. tsuchida et al. [6] demonstrated in dogs with experimentally induced ischemia that tea attenuated the s-t segment elevation, the myocardial lactate production, and the decrease in subendocardial ph. vikmo et al. [7] were able to reverse ischemic s-t segment changes from coronary occlusion in a canine model with tea. davis et al. [8] demonstrated improved regional endocardial perfusion and a smaller infarct using tea in a dog model with experimentally induced ischemia. klassen et al. [9] found that coronary blood flow during tea was redistributed in favor of the endocardium in normal and ischemic dog hearts. kock et al. [10] examined the effect of tea on the determinants of myocardial oxygen supply and demand during exercise stress tests in patients receiving beta-adrenergic blockers. the same patients underwent two stress tests, the first without tea and the second with tea. the patients had larger efs, fewer regional wall motion abnormalities, and less significant s-t segment depression during the exercise stress test with tea than during the test without tea. they also had lower rate-pressure products, lower systolic pressures, and lower diastolic pressures when receiving tea during the test. detrimental effects of tea on myocardial supply may result from decreased preload if the sympathectomy extends beyond the distribution of the high thoracic dermatomes (t1-t5). for this reason, we ensure that the position of the epidural catheter tip is at the t1-t3 level with an epidurogram. there is also a report of s-t segment elevation occurring during thoracic surgery under tea, which was attributed to coronary vasospasm from unopposed vagal tone [11]. another concern is whether the coronary vasodilation resulting from the sympathectomy causes coronary steal. blomberg et al. [4] measured an increase in the diameter of stenotic vessels during tea, but no such dilation in the nonstenotic segments in humans. this response was limited to epicardial vessels. the use of thoracic epidural infusion for control of pain after an acute myocardial infarction is not without precedent. toft and jorgensen [12] used continuous tea with 0.25% bupivacaine at an infusion rate of 6.1 ml/h to control pain in 14 patients for 12 to 42 h. we chose to continue epidural anesthesia during surgery because of the benefits from tea on intraoperative hemodynamic parameters, postoperative recovery, and the stress response to surgery. liem et al. [2] found that tea during cab surgery in patients with efs more than 40% improved myocardial blood flow, decreased myocardial oxygen demand, and dilated stenosed arteries intraoperatively. this study also found more stable hemodynamic parameters during separation from bypass with tea when compared with patients receiving general anesthesia alone. the intraoperative and postoperative stress response was decreased in the tea group, as measured by a combination of plasma cortisol, norepinephrine, and epinephrine levels [13]. postoperatively, patients in the tea group were extubated sooner, had better visual analog scores for pain, and a lower incidence of tachycardia and myocardial ischemia [14]. kirno et al. [15] confirmed these findings by showing that the addition of tea to general anesthesia during cab surgery in patients with efs greater than 50% reduced the sympathetic stress response to sternotomy, as measured by plasma norepinephrine levels and hemodynamic parameters, when compared with general anesthesia alone. epidural hematoma is an uncommon but potentially catastrophic complication of epidural catheter placement in patients undergoing systemic anticoagulation. rao and el-etr [16] found no epidural hematomas among 3164 patients who received epidural anesthesia and perioperative iv heparin for peripheral vascular surgery. rough and dougherty [17], however, noted seven spinal hematomas in 342 anticoagulated patients undergoing continuous spinal anesthesia and found that aspirin therapy, therapeutic anticoagulation within 1 hour of catheter insertion, and traumatic catheter insertion were risk factors for hematomas. although our patient was taking aspirin throughout his stabilization period, horlocker et al. [18] have determined the contribution of antiplatelet drugs to the risk of epidural hematoma to be minimal. we allowed this patient's partial thromboplastin time to normalize prior to catheter insertion and placed the catheter well in advance of the 24 h advocated in the literature [19] before systemic heparinization for cardiopulmonary bypass. the risk of infarction after stopping a heparin infusion, albeit temporarily, in patients with unstable angina is great and must be considered on a case-by-case basis. our patient's symptoms did not worsen after heparin withdrawal and heparin was not restarted after catheter placement because tea relieved the pain completely. although we have no echocardiographic or other direct evidence that tea improved his ischemic cardiomyopathy, normal myocardial enzyme panels obtained after initiating tea and the complete relief of symptoms suggest there was no infarct progression. our patient's intraoperative course was characterized by stable hemodynamic parameters with minimal inotropic or vasoactive drug support. he required no postoperative iv opioids for pain. we did not encounter evidence of decreased preload or coronary vasospasm during the course of tea. studies using bolus dosing of the epidural catheter at preset intervals have found that the dosing interval may be increased with time and that the pain-free interval outlasts the duration of drug effect [20]. since we used a continuous infusion of local anesthetic in this patient, we cannot substantiate these findings. we find angina prophylaxis with a continuous infusion more effective than bolus administration in patients who become panicked at the onset of angina. we have not noted tachyphylaxis in patients who have had their infusions running continuously for up to 36 days, but this is undergoing further study. there is evidence that an alpha2-agonist-mediated sympathectomy may provide an alternative to tea for protection from myocardial ischemia. ellis and colleagues [21] found that clonidine premedication lessened intraoperative myocardial ischemia in noncardiac surgery, whereas dorman et al. [22] found less s-t segment depression during the sternotomy to cross-clamp period in patients premedicated with clonidine for cab surgery. the smooth operative course reported herein suggests that the benefits of tea derived from studies of patients with preserved left ventricular function may be extrapolated to patients with lower efs. this case further substantiates the role of tea in the management of patients with severe ischemic heart disease. a close working relationship among cardiac anesthesiologists, cardiologists, and cardiothoracic surgeons is essential for success with this therapy.

title: trends in workplace wearable technologies and connected worker solutions for next generation occupational safety, health, and productivity
display_name: Trends in Workplace Wearable Technologies and Connected‐Worker Solutions for Next‐Generation Occupational Safety, Health, and Productivity
abstract: the workplace influences the safety, health, and productivity of workers at multiple levels. to protect and promote total worker health, smart hardware, and software tools have emerged for the identification, elimination, substitution, and control of occupational hazards. wearable devices enable constant monitoring of individual workers and the environment, whereas connected worker solutions provide contextual information and decision support. here, the recent trends in commercial workplace technologies to monitor and manage occupational risks, injuries, accidents, and diseases are reviewed. workplace safety wearables for safe lifting, ergonomics, hazard identification, sleep monitoring, fatigue management, and heat and cold stress are discussed. examples of workplace productivity wearables for asset tracking, augmented reality, gesture and motion control, brain wave sensing, and work stress management are given. workplace health wearables designed for work related musculoskeletal disorders, functional movement disorders, respiratory hazards, cardiovascular health, outdoor sun exposure, and continuous glucose monitoring are shown. connected worker platforms are discussed with information about the architecture, system modules, intelligent operations, and industry applications. predictive analytics provide contextual information about occupational safety risks, resource allocation, equipment failure, and predictive maintenance. altogether, these examples highlight the ground level benefits of real time visibility about frontline workers, work environment, distributed assets, workforce efficiency, and safety compliance.

title: management of post-intubation tracheal stenoses using the endoscopic approach

institutions: Azienda Socio Sanitaria Territoriale degli Spedali Civili di Brescia

abstract: background and aim. tracheal stenosis is a common complication of intubation with or without subsequent tracheotomy whose management remains poorly defined. over 600 post-intubation tracheal stenoses have been treated in our centre since 1982: the aim of this study was to determine the safety and efficacy of our endoscopic approach. methods. this retrospective study includes 113 new cases treated between 1998 and 2001. we chose this period to have a standardised technique and a significant number of cases with a sufficiently long follow up (28-78 months). forty patients who did not meet the criteria for true stenosis (granulomas, pseudoglottic stenosis, etc.) were excluded from the study. results. 73 patients (50 21 years) entered the study: 13 (18%) web-like and 60 (82%) complex stenoses. most web-like stenoses were successfully treated with laser assisted mechanical dilation (lamd) alone; among complex stenoses lamd was sufficient to treat 13 patients (22%), whereas 47 patients (78%) required stent placement: 22 had their stent removed after one year and did not require any further therapy, 13 inoperable patients required permanent stent and 12 were referred to surgery after failure of multiple endoscopic treatments. no permanent complications secondary to endoscopic treatment were observed. 48 patients (66%) obtained a stable, good result with the endoscopic procedure, 13 (18%) required a permanent stent while 12 patients (16%) were referred to surgery. conclusions. our results indicate that the endoscopic treatment of post-intubation tracheal stenoses performed in an expert setting can be considered a safe first-line therapy, leaving some selected cases and the relapsing stenoses, for surgical resection.
